title: CalCo: A Hierarchical Bayesian Framework for Scalable Human-LLM Hybrid Labeling

problem.claim: Hybrid annotation systems need to incorporate non-deterministic LLM-generated labels alongside human labels, including in settings with multiple correlated tasks and diverse model architectures.

gap.claim: Existing human labeling processes lack an effective way to incorporate non-deterministic LLM signals in complex industrial settings.

contributions.claim: CalCo is a system for integrating LLM and human labels at scale.
CalCo uses a hierarchical Bayesian model that captures dependencies across multi-task, multi-LLM annotation processes.
CalCo jointly models dependencies across related tasks and correlations among diverse LLMs to share statistical strength and capture shared model error profiles.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors describe the hierarchical Bayesian model as novel.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report extensive empirical results on simulated and real-world datasets.
The authors report that CalCo significantly outperforms baseline methods across a wide range of applications.

narrative_sequence.summary: LLMs are shifting annotation workflows toward hybrid systems combining human and LLM-generated labels.
Incorporating non-deterministic LLM signals remains difficult in complex multi-task settings with diverse models.
CalCo integrates LLM and human labels in a system deployed at scale.
Its hierarchical Bayesian model jointly represents task dependencies and correlations among LLMs.
The authors report improved performance over baselines on simulated and real-world datasets.

source_observation.claim: The approach jointly models related tasks and correlations among diverse LLMs.

interpretation.claim: Sharing information across tasks and models may help exploit common structure and error patterns.

application.claim: Hybrid labeling systems with correlated tasks or multiple models could consider joint probabilistic modeling instead of isolated input treatment.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether joint modeling helps when tasks or model errors are weakly related.

unknowns: The abstract does not provide quantitative performance improvements.
The abstract does not identify the datasets, baselines, tasks, or application domains.
The abstract does not describe deployment scale or computational requirements.
